opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so, GPT-5 was a modest update for me, and if anything it pushed me a little toward longer timelines rather than shorter ones.

Some context: when we wrote AI 2027, 2027 was roughly my modal year for when things really start to go crazy, meaning automation of AI research itself, but my median was already a bit later than that. Even then I was saying there's a lot of uncertainty. Since then my median has drifted out somewhat, maybe to around 2029-ish, though I hold that loosely.

GPT-5 was basically on trend. It wasn't a huge discontinuous leap the way GPT-4 felt relative to GPT-3.5. It was a solid improvement, especially on agentic coding tasks and the length of tasks models can do autonomously. If you look at the METR-style horizon-length graphs, it landed roughly where you'd expect if the trend continues, maybe a bit above.

So on one hand, "on trend" is actually kind of scary, because the trend is exponential and points to systems that can do multi-week or multi-month projects within a few years. On the other hand, some people, me included to a degree, had put some probability on things going faster than trend, with labs having big surprises in store. GPT-5 didn't deliver that kind of surprise, so I shifted a bit of probability mass away from the fastest scenarios.

The question I care about most isn't how impressive the chatbot is. It's when AI can substantially speed up AI research, because that's when you get the intelligence explosion dynamics we describe in the scenario. GPT-5 and its contemporaries are useful to researchers, but we're not yet at the point where they're doing the core research work. So I'm watching the agentic benchmarks, the horizon-length metrics, and reports from inside labs about how much the models actually accelerate their own work.

The headline is: slightly longer timelines, but not dramatically, and I still think there's a substantial chance, maybe a third or more, that we get something like superhuman coders before the end of the decade. That's still incredibly soon given how unprepared we are, so the strategic upshot hasn't changed much. We need to be working on alignment, transparency, and governance now, not waiting for some fire alarm.

r001.rationale: The candidate says some had assigned probability to progress going faster than trend, and GPT-5 did not deliver that surprise, so they shifted probability away from the fastest scenarios and slightly toward longer timelines.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so GPT-5 was interesting for me because it was a bit of a nothing-burger relative to what some people were expecting, and I'd say it nudged my timelines somewhat longer. Not dramatically, but noticeably.

So for context, when we wrote AI 2027 earlier that year, our modal scenario had things going quite fast, with the superhuman coder milestone hitting around early 2027. And my actual median was always a bit later than the scenario, because the scenario is sort of the "this is what it looks like if things go roughly on the faster side of what we think is plausible" story. But GPT-5 was one of the data points that pushed me to think, okay, the trend is probably continuing, but it's continuing at something more like the historical pace than the accelerated pace that the scenario was depicting.

A couple of things specifically. One is that it didn't feel like a big jump in general intelligence. It felt like a consolidation release — better routing between models, better at coding, fewer hallucinations, that sort of thing. The benchmarks moved, but in a way that was consistent with the trends we were already tracking, not a break upward. The METR time horizon stuff, for example, kept doubling at roughly the rate it had been, which is actually the important thing. If the time horizon doubling were speeding up, that would be the signal that we're getting close to the point where AI starts substantially accelerating AI research. And it wasn't obviously speeding up.

The second thing is the broader vibe around it. OpenAI clearly wanted this to be a big moment, and it kind of wasn't. That tells you something about how much of the low-hanging fruit from pretraining scaling has been picked, and that the remaining gains are coming more from RL on reasoning and agentic tasks, which is a slower, grindier process. Not slow in absolute terms, but it's not the kind of thing where you wake up one morning and the model is dramatically smarter.

So where did that leave me? I'd say my median for something like the superhuman coder milestone moved from roughly 2027 to roughly 2028 or 2029, and my distribution got a bit wider. I want to be careful here though — it's not like I've become a skeptic. The trends are still really fast by any historical standard. Every year the models get meaningfully better at long-horizon agentic tasks, and that's the thing that matters for the automation-of-AI-research story. And I'd say a lot of people overcorrected in the other direction after GPT-5, like "oh, the scaling is over, the bubble is popping." That's not what the data says either. It says the trend lines are intact, and the trend lines still point at something pretty wild happening in the next several years.

The other lesson I took from it is epistemic. I think I and others should have been putting more weight on the scenario where progress continues at trend rather than accelerating, and I'm trying to be more disciplined about updating on the actual measured metrics rather than on the hype cycle around individual releases. Any single model release is a fairly noisy signal. What you want to look at is the slope over a couple years.

r001.rationale: The candidate says GPT-5 did not show the accelerated progress depicted in a plausible faster scenario and that this data point nudged their timelines somewhat longer.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between “How impressive is this particular release?” and “How soon can AI automate AI research?” The second question is much more central to my timelines. You can have a model that feels like an incremental improvement in ordinary conversation but is substantially more useful for coding and running experiments.

So I wouldn’t treat GPT-5’s release, by itself, as a decisive reason to move timelines forward or backward. I’d want to see how reliably it can do longer tasks, how much human supervision it needs, and whether researchers can actually use it to accelerate their work. Those are the things that would make me update substantially.

r001.rationale: The response does not say GPT-5 failed to deliver a previously plausible acceleration or treat that as slight evidence for longer timelines. It says the release alone is not decisive and names factors that would prompt an update.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between how impressive a model feels in conversation and how close it is to automating AI research. The second is much more important for my timelines. Can it carry out a research project, notice when an experiment has gone wrong, and keep making progress without someone constantly steering it?

So I wouldn’t treat GPT-5’s release, by itself, as a reason for a dramatic update. What would move me much more is evidence about how reliably it can do that kind of sustained work. A model can be very impressive and still fall short of that threshold.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-5’s release alone is not a reason for a dramatic update, but does not identify its failure to deliver a plausible acceleration as slight evidence for longer timelines.
